v.q: A `@Scheduled` job runs in a service deployed on three instances. What happens by default?
o: It runs on all three instances at the same time
Spring elects one instance to run it each time
Only the first instance to start will ever run it
It does not run at all when deployed in a cluster
v.w: Each JVM has its own scheduler, so the job fires on every instance. You need a lock or a central scheduler to run it once.

v.q: Which statement about @Scheduled on a service with three instances is NOT true?
o: Spring elects one instance to run the job
Each JVM has its own scheduler
The job fires on every instance
A shared lock is needed to run it once
v.w: Spring has no leader election for @Scheduled. Every instance fires its own timer.

v.q: Which approach makes a scheduled job run on only one instance per tick?
o: A distributed lock such as ShedLock, or Quartz clustering
A larger thread pool for the scheduler
Switching from `cron` to `fixedRate` timing
Marking the scheduled method `synchronized`
v.w: `synchronized` only works inside one JVM. A shared lock (database row, Redis key) coordinates across instances.

v.q: Why does marking a scheduled method synchronized not stop a second instance from running it?
o: synchronized locks only inside one JVM
Synchronized methods cannot be scheduled
The cron expression ignores locks
Spring removes the keyword at startup
v.w: A monitor is local to one process. A cross-instance lock needs a shared store such as a database row or Redis key.

v.q: A lock holder crashes without releasing the lock. How do distributed locks avoid blocking the job forever?
o: The lock has a lease or TTL and expires on its own
Another instance forcibly kills the holder process
The lock is never held for longer than a millisecond
The database drops the lock table after a minute
v.w: Locks use `lockAtMostFor` (ShedLock) or a Redis TTL. Set it longer than the normal job duration but short enough to recover.

v.q: Which setting stops a crashed lock holder from blocking a job forever?
o: A lease or TTL such as lockAtMostFor
A larger thread pool
A shorter cron interval
The synchronized keyword
v.w: The lock expires on its own after the lease, so another instance can take over.

v.q: A job holds a lock with a 30-second lease but occasionally runs 45 seconds. What is the risk?
o: The lease expires and a second instance starts the same job
The database cancels the long-running job
The lock silently becomes permanent
Nothing, because the lock extends itself
v.w: Make the job idempotent and either extend the lease while running or use a fencing token so a stale holder cannot do damage.

v.q: A job with a 30-second lease sometimes needs 45 seconds. Which fix is NOT sensible?
o: Make the lease 5 seconds
Extend the lease while the job runs
Use a fencing token
Make the job idempotent
v.w: A shorter lease makes overlap more likely. Fix the gap with a longer or renewed lease, a fencing token and idempotent work.

v.q: Why should scheduled jobs be idempotent?
o: Jobs can run twice or be retried, and the result must stay correct
Idempotent jobs always execute faster than others
Cron expressions require idempotent code to parse
It avoids the need for a database altogether
v.w: At-least-once execution is the realistic guarantee. Use a unique business key or processed marker so a rerun does no extra harm.

v.q: Which statement about idempotent scheduled jobs is NOT true?
o: They make a rerun unnecessary because exactly-once is guaranteed
They stay correct when a run is repeated
A processed marker can make them idempotent
They help when a retry follows a crash
v.w: At-least-once is the realistic guarantee, which is why a rerun must be safe.

v.q: What is the difference between `fixedRate` and `fixedDelay` in Spring?
o: `fixedRate` counts from each start, `fixedDelay` from the previous end
`fixedRate` is only valid when written as a cron-style string
`fixedDelay` runs several jobs in parallel threads by default
They behave identically in every situation that you meet
v.w: Use `fixedDelay` when runs must not overlap in time. `fixedRate` can queue up or overlap if a run is slow.

v.q: A report job must not start again until the previous run ends, even if one run is slow. Which setting fits?
o: fixedDelay
fixedRate
A shorter cron expression
A larger thread pool
v.w: fixedDelay counts from the end of the last run. fixedRate counts from each start and can overlap.

v.q: A nightly batch has 10 million rows to process. What scales best across instances?
o: Split the work into partitions that workers claim independently
Let one instance do everything while the others idle
Run the same full job on every instance at once
Process one row per minute to stay safe
v.w: Partitioning (by id range or hash) lets instances share the load. Claim rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or a status column.

v.q: Which approach to processing 10 million rows across instances is NOT sensible?
o: Run the full job on every instance at once
Split the rows into partitions
Claim rows with SKIP LOCKED
Use a status column to mark claimed work
v.w: Running everything everywhere duplicates work. Partitioning lets instances share the load.

v.q: Which is a benefit of a dedicated scheduler service (for example Quartz cluster or a workflow engine) over per-service `@Scheduled`?
o: Central persistence, misfire handling and a visible job history
No configuration is needed at all
Retries are no longer necessary
Jobs automatically run exactly once without any extra care
v.w: Persistent job stores let jobs survive restarts and let you inspect, pause and retrigger them. Exactly-once still needs idempotent job code.

v.q: Which feature of a dedicated scheduler such as Quartz cluster helps after a restart?
o: Persistent jobs and misfire handling
No retries are ever needed
Jobs always run exactly once
No database is needed
v.w: A persistent job store lets jobs survive restarts and lets you inspect and retrigger them.
